title: The Great Trap
summary: Punish a mistaken rook check with a king retreat, while distinguishing the source’s winning trap from the drawn original diagram.

nodes.question: Which king move preserves the win after Black’s mistaken check?
nodes.explanation: The original diagram is drawn. Black’s ...Rb2+ changes that result; now Ke1 is the only winning reply.

nodes.question: Does the initial diagram force a win?
nodes.explanation: No. The tablebase evaluates the original seven-piece position as drawn. Black must choose a drawing rook defense after Rb8 rather than the video’s ...Rb2+.

branches.title: Offer the rook and bring the king around
commentary: Begin after Rb8 Rb2+, the source’s losing check for Black. White must now find the one winning king reply.
Ke1 retreats from the check without disturbing the mating plan. The king will approach via d1 and c1.
Rxb8 accepts White’s rook offer, but gives the bishop a forcing check.
Bd4+ checks along d4-c3-b2-a1.
Rb2 is forced to block that diagonal. Black’s king cannot move, its pawn is blocked, and its light-squared bishop cannot block a dark-squared diagonal.
Kd1 heads toward c1, where the king can protect b2.
Bf5 is the illustrated waiting move. The other black pieces remain trapped.
Kc1 reaches the square needed to protect Bxb2.
Be6 is another illustrated waiting move. The bishop cannot protect b2 or check the king on c1 from its color complex.
Bxb2# captures the blocking rook and checks Ka1. Kc1 protects the bishop and covers b1; Black’s own a2 pawn blocks a2.
branches.explanation: Bxb2# captures the blocking rook and checks Ka1. Kc1 protects the bishop and covers b1; Black’s own a2 pawn blocks a2.

branches.title: The immediate bishop check draws
commentary: The source correctly identifies the direct bishop check as drawn. The original diagram itself is also drawn with best play.
Bd4+ holds a draw. It does not throw away a win from the original diagram, because that diagram has no forced White win.
Rxd4+ captures the bishop with a countercheck along the d-file.
Rxd4 recaptures the rook, but White no longer has the bishop needed for the mating cage.
Kb2 frees the a-pawn’s promotion square. The exact rook-versus-bishop-and-pawn position is drawn with best play.
branches.explanation: Kb2 frees the a-pawn’s promotion square. The exact rook-versus-bishop-and-pawn position is drawn with best play.

branches.title: Accept Black’s rook offer
commentary: Black’s ...Rb2+ has given White a win, but accepting the checking rook gives it back.
Rxb2 gives up the forced win. White abandons the rook that was needed to force the mating arrangement.
Kxb2 captures the rook, freeing the a-pawn. White’s remaining bishop can hold the exact position to a draw, but cannot force the source’s mate.
branches.explanation: Kxb2 captures the rook, freeing the a-pawn. White’s remaining bishop can hold the exact position to a draw, but cannot force the source’s mate.

branches.title: Black preserves the original draw
commentary: The quiet rook offer is a good practical trap, but does not force a win against accurate defense.
Rb8 retains the drawn evaluation. Black must avoid the source’s losing ...Rb2+ or ...Rxb8.
Ra4 is an independently checked representative drawing defense. Black keeps the rook active on the fourth rank rather than entering White’s mating construction.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Ra4 is an independently checked representative drawing defense. Black keeps the rook active on the fourth rank rather than entering White’s mating construction.

exercises.prompt: Why is Ke1 useful despite moving away?
exercises.answer: After Black’s losing ...Rb2+, Ke1 is the only winning reply. It preserves the cage and lets White approach via d1 and c1 after the rook blocks Bd4+.

exercises.prompt: Why can Black’s bishop not stop Bxb2 mate?
exercises.answer: It moves on the opposite color from White’s bishop and b2. Once White’s king reaches c1, it protects the mating bishop and covers b1.

startContext: Begin after Rb8 Rb2+ at 74 seconds. The original seven-piece diagram is drawn; Black’s checking reply is the error that permits White’s win. Both the original diagram and a representative drawing defense are checked alongside the selected mating line.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.

sourceCorrections.claim: White can force an incredible win from the initial diagram by playing Rb8.
sourceCorrections.correction: The original diagram and Rb8 are drawn with best play. Black can preserve the draw with ...Ra4, among other fourth-rank rook moves. The illustrated ...Rb2+ instead loses, after which Ke1 is the only winning move. The practice root therefore begins after that mistake.
